extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, agency staff, regulated parties, public commenters, and researchers searching Federal Register documents about endangerment findings and related notices
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register search-results listing of documents matching the term 'endangerment finding', including titles, abstracts, and excerpts from EPA, FWS, NMFS, and other agencies describing 90-day and 12-month petition findings, proposed/rescission rules, notices, and procedural deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90-day petition finding standard (ESA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must determine whether a petition presents "substantial scientific or commercial information indicating that the petitioned action may be warranted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding is made within 90 days of receipt of the petition to the maximum extent practicable and published promptly in the Federal Register. A positive 90-day finding triggers initiation of a status review; a negative finding ends the immediate action but may be reopened if new information is submitted. Example wording from results: "we find that the petitions ... present substantial scientific or commercial information indicating that the petitioned actions may be warranted."

rubrics_metrics.name: 12-month petition finding standard (ESA)
rubrics_metrics.description: After a status review, the agency issues a 12-month finding based on the "best scientific and commercial data available" whether listing the species as endangered or threatened is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible 12-month outcomes include: warranted (propose to list), not warranted (no listing), or warranted-but-precluded. The finding must be supported by a thorough review of the best available data and is documented in the administrative record. Example phrasing: "After a thorough review of the best scientific and commercial data available, we find that listing ... is not warranted at this time."

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger for initiating status review
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive 90-day finding (substantial information) requires the agency to initiate a status review to determine whether the petitioned action is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status reviews solicit scientific and commercial data and other information to be comprehensive. The search excerpts show the sequence: positive 90-day finding → initiation of status review → 12-month finding. Agencies request public input/data to inform the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical habitat petition 90-day standard and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: For petitions to revise critical habitat designations, the Act requires the agency to make a finding on whether the petition presents substantial scientific information indicating the petitioned action may be warranted, generally within 90 days and publish the finding in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies state: "To the maximum extent practicable, we are to make this finding within 90 days of our receipt of the petition and publish the finding promptly in the Federal Register." The same 'substantial information' threshold applies to critical-habitat petitions as to listing petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the administrative record and handling of resubmitted petitions (CNOR practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual candidate notices of review (CNOR) and resubmitted-petition findings may supersede earlier findings; prior findings remain part of the administrative record and may be relied upon or incorporated by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies explain that new annual findings "supersede the earlier findings, although all previous findings are part of the administrative record for the new finding, and in the new finding, we may rely upon them or include them by reference as appropriate, in addition to explaining why the finding has changed."

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment and docket procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices indicate where and by when the public must submit comments (deadlines, docket numbers, web links) and when comment periods are extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the results: extension notices that state exact new comment deadlines (e.g., "Comments must be received on or before September 22, 2025"), instructions to identify comments by docket number, and links to supporting documents in the docket. Timeliness and docket identification are required for comments to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for 'not determinable' or 'not-warranted' outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When data are insufficient or the best available data do not support listing or critical-habitat designation, agencies may issue a 'not determinable' or 'not warranted' finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies state reasons such as insufficient information, or that available data do not indicate that statutory criteria are met. Example phrasing: "designating critical habitat for this species is not determinable at this time" and "we find that listing ... is not warranted at this time."

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/statutory interpretation criteria for endangerment findings under the Clean Air Act (CAA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Endangerment determinations under CAA section 202(a) depend on interpreting statutory terms such as "air pollution," "cause," "contribute," and "reasonably be anticipated to endanger," and may consider doctrines like the major questions doctrine and whether the statute authorizes particular emission standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA documents in the results articulate analytic steps: evaluate the 'best reading' of section 202(a), examine meanings of statutory terms, consider reliance interests and legal doctrines (e.g., major questions), and determine whether emissions and standards materially impact public health and welfare. Example from results: "best reading of the statutory terms 'air pollution,' 'cause,' 'contribute,' and 'reasonably be anticipated to endanger.'"

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for rescission or repeal of prior findings/standards (EPA approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency proposing to rescind an earlier endangerment finding or repeal standards must identify bases such as lack of statutory authority, flaws in prior scientific analysis, changed developments casting doubt on reliability, or that available technology cannot address concerns without greater harms to public health and welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's proposed rationales in the search results include: (1) best reading of statutory authority does not support standards; (2) prior findings were unreasonably analyzed; (3) developments cast doubt on reliability; (4) no requisite technology can address concerns without risking greater harms. Each basis must be supported and explained in the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to publish findings and supporting documents in Federal Register and docket
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency findings, proposed rules, and notices must be published in the Federal Register with links to supporting documents in the public docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search results repeatedly include 'Supporting documents can be found in the docket for this rule' and provide html/pdf URLs and public-inspection PDFs. Publication provides the formal record for notice-and-comment and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional responsibility statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies state their statutory responsibility to make listing or endangerment determinations for species or pollutants within their jurisdiction (e.g., NMFS for marine species, FWS for terrestrial species, EPA for air pollutants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The search excerpts state roles such as 'NMFS is responsible for determining whether species under its jurisdiction are threatened or endangered under the ESA' — these jurisdictional assignments determine which statutory procedures and standards apply.
